author_claim: In Romans 4:3, the Greek term ἐλογίσθη employs a financial accounting metaphor meaning 'was set down on the credit side.'
short_quote: metaphor from accounts, 'was set down,' here 'on the credit side.'
source_locator: Commentary on Rom 4:3, p. 100 (PDF slice p. 12)
qualification: Sanday & Headlam note legal usage in LXX for imputation of guilt (Lev 7:8, 17:4). Secondary historical commentary.

author_claim: Paul maintains a stricter adherence to the text of Genesis 15:6 than James by focusing exclusively on faith rather than appealing to later narrative events like the offering of Isaac.
short_quote: We notice at once that St. Paul keeps more strictly to his text. Gen. xv. 6 speaks only of faith.
source_locator: Note on Rom 4:7-8 / Gen 15:6, p. 102 (PDF slice p. 14)
qualification: Authors note James supports works by appealing to later Gen 22 Isaac incident.

author_claim: In Romans 9:25 (second clause), Paul seems to have used a Septuagint text containing the reading of Codex Vaticanus (B, ἀγαπήσω τὴν οὐκ ἠγαπημένην) rather than the majority LXX reading (ἐλεήσω τὴν οὐκ ἠλεημένην).
short_quote: In the second clause St. Paul seems to have used a text containing the reading of the Vatican MS., for the latter can hardly have been altered to harmonize with him.
source_locator: Commentary on Rom 9:25-26, p. 264 (PDF slice p. 15)
qualification: Sanday & Headlam frame this as a probable textual inference ('seems to have used'), observing that Codex Vaticanus can hardly have been retrospectively altered to harmonize with Paul. Secondary commentary hypothesis on textual transmission.
notes: Visibly verified on printed p. 264. Self-audit correction incorporated: preserves author's explicit hedging.

author_claim: In Romans 9:25, Paul inverts the order of the Hosea 2:23 clauses so that the reference to τὸν οὐ λαόν μου comes first; the verb καλέσω naturally crept in from ἐκάλεσεν in v. 24 (changing the construction to a double accusative meaning 'I will name'), with Sanday & Headlam explaining this verbal assimilation as an incidental psychological habit rather than inferring deliberate theological substitution.
short_quote: St. Paul inverts the order of the clauses ... and for ἐρῶ substitutes καλέσω which naturally crept in from the ἐκάλεσεν of the previous verse, and changes the construction of the clause to suit the new word.
source_locator: Commentary on Rom 9:25, p. 264 (PDF slice p. 15)
qualification: Authors describe καλέσω as naturally creeping in via verbal assimilation from v. 24, requiring a double accusative construction meaning 'I will name'; framing against deliberate theological substitution is an inference from the authors' 'naturally crept in' account.
notes: Visibly verified on printed p. 264. Self-audit correction incorporated: captures exact observed mechanism.

author_claim: The primary textual divergence between Paul's quotation of Hosea 1:10 in Romans 9:26 and the Septuagint is Paul's insertion of ἐκεῖ to stress the locus of divine reception.
short_quote: The only difference between St. Paul's quotation and the LXX is that he inserts ἐκεῖ :this insertion seems to emphasize the idea of the place
source_locator: Commentary on Rom 9:26, p. 264 (PDF slice p. 15)
qualification: Authors present two alternative interpretations of 'place': Palestine/Jerusalem vs universal earth.

author_claim: Paul adds the universal quantifier πᾶς ('everyone') to his quotation of Isaiah 28:16 in Romans 10:11 to prove that faith in Christ is the universal condition of salvation for Jews and Gentiles alike.
short_quote: Quoted from Is. xxviii. 16 (see above, ix. 33) with the addition of πᾶς to bring out the point on which emphasis is to be laid.
source_locator: Commentary on Rom 10:11, p. 290 (PDF slice p. 23)
qualification: Connects back to Rom 9:33 where πᾶς was absent.

author_claim: In Romans 10:13, Paul's quotation of Joel 2:32 (LXX 3:5) agrees with both the LXX and the Hebrew texts in wording and meaning as assessed by the authors, with the divine name Κύριος applied christologically to Jesus Christ.
short_quote: the quotation agrees with both the LXX and the Hebrew texts ... The term Κύριος is applied to Christ by St. Paul in this connection.
source_locator: Commentary on Rom 10:13, p. 291 (PDF slice p. 24)
qualification: Original text refers to Jehovah in day of the Lord; applied christologically to Christian salvation. Wording follows authors' assessment ('agrees with both') avoiding cross-language verbatim claim.

author_claim: Paul cites Isaiah 40:13 in Romans 11:34 with only slight variation from the Septuagint to confirm the unsearchable depth of God's wisdom and judgments.
short_quote: This is taken from Is. xl. 13, varying only very slightly from the LXX. It is quoted also 1 Cor. ii. 16.
source_locator: Commentary on Rom 11:34, p. 340 (PDF slice p. 31)
qualification: Contrasted with v. 35 (Job 41:11) which varies considerably from LXX.

author_claim: Paul's citation of Isaiah 11:10 in Romans 15:12 adopts the Septuagint's paraphrastic rendering to describe the Messianic reign of the 'root of Jesse' over the Gentiles.
short_quote: The quotation follows the LXX, which is only a paraphrase of the Hebrew
source_locator: Commentary on Rom 15:12, p. 399 (PDF slice p. 35)
qualification: Compares LXX ὁ ἀνιστάμενος ἄρχειν ἐθνῶν with Hebrew MT ('which standeth for an ensign').

author_claim: Sanday and Headlam report Emil Kautzsch's (1869) statistical classification of 84 Pauline quotations: ~70 are taken directly from or closely match the LXX, 12 vary considerably but show affinity, and only two (both from Job: Rom 11:35 and 1 Cor 3:19) are definitely independent of the LXX.
short_quote: out of eighty-four passages in which St. Paul cites the O. T. about seventy are taken directly from the LXX or do not vary from it appreciably, twelve vary considerably, but still show signs of affinity, and two only... are definitely independent
source_locator: Excursus: 'St. Paul's Use of the Old Testament', p. 302 (PDF slice p. 25)
qualification: Nineteenth-century statistical taxonomy reported from Kautzsch (1869); historical scholarly classification, not established modern textual consensus.

author_claim: Where Pauline quotations derived from the Septuagint show points of resemblance to the Hebrew text against the LXX (e.g. Rom 10:15), Sanday and Headlam judge that evidence is insufficient to decide between Hebrew memory (conscious or unconscious), an Aramaic Targum, or an earlier form of the LXX text.
short_quote: We have probably not sufficient evidence to say whether this arises from a reminiscence of the Hebrew text (conscious or unconscious), or from an Aramaic Targum, or from the use of an earlier form of a LXX text.
source_locator: Excursus: 'St. Paul's Use of the Old Testament', p. 302 (PDF slice p. 25)
qualification: Explicit recognition of explanatory uncertainty and textual limits in 1895 scholarship.

author_claim: Sanday and Headlam judge that the majority of Paul's Old Testament quotations are made from memory rather than transcribed by reference, citing their brevity and frequent inexactness in marked contrast to the literary citations in Hebrews.
short_quote: it may be safely said that the majority of the quotations are from memory; for many of them are somewhat inexact, and those which are correct are for the most part short and from well-known books. There is a very marked distinction between these and the long literary quotations of the Epistle to the Hebrews.
source_locator: Excursus: 'St. Paul's Use of the Old Testament', p. 302 (PDF slice p. 25)
qualification: Authors' compositional hypothesis contrasting Pauline habit with the Epistle to the Hebrews.

author_claim: Sanday and Headlam state that Paul's exegesis is not 'historical' in the modern sense because passages are quoted without regard to original context or circumstances, including instances where Old Testament words are applied in an opposite sense (e.g. Rom 9:25–26 applying words spoken of the ten tribes to the Gentiles).
short_quote: In the first place it is quite clearly not 'historical' in the modern sense of the word. The passages are quoted without regard to their context or to the circumstances under which they were written. The most striking instances of this are those cases in which the words of the O. T. are used in an exactly opposite sense
source_locator: Excursus: 'St. Paul's Use of the Old Testament', p. 303 (PDF slice p. 26)
qualification: Distinguishes non-contextual application from rabbinic allegory; notes Paul's method remains broadly literal in verbal meaning rather than allegorical.
notes: Visibly verified on printed p. 303. Cross-reference: covers both Rom 9:25 (B001-2) and Rom 9:26 (B001-3) in opposite-sense application of Hosea 1-2 to Gentiles.

author_claim: Sanday and Headlam distinguish Paul's theological insight into the spiritual and Messianic meaning of the Old Testament from his historical exegesis, holding that modern scholars are not bound by historically incorrect exegesis of particular passages while affirming the reality of the universal Messianic idea.
short_quote: We are not bound, and it would be wrong to bind ourselves, by the incorrect exegesis of particular passages; but the reality and truth of the Messianic idea and the universal character of the Messianic kingdom... remain one of the most real and impressive facts in religious history.
source_locator: Excursus: 'St. Paul's Use of the Old Testament', p. 306 (PDF slice p. 29)
qualification: Authors' theological-hermeneutical judgment reconciling apostolic authority with modern historical-critical methods. Explicitly cites C. H. Toy (1884), B. Jowett, E. Kautzsch (1869), A. Clemen (1891), and D. M. Turpie (1868).
